title: Telemetry ingestion lag during worker instability

evidence.text: A new telemetry schema increased median event size by 41% and introduced a nested attribute map parsed by the ingest decoder.
Within 12 minutes of enabling the schema, ingest-worker allocation rate increased 2.3x and full-GC pauses rose from under 100 ms to 9-14 s.
Broker lease duration is 10 s. During full-GC pauses, affected workers stopped heartbeating and 18% of in-flight messages were redelivered.
Redelivered messages carried the same broker message IDs as their first deliveries.
The deduplication service CPU exceeded 95% only after redelivery volume rose; before that point it remained below 50%.
Customer-visible ingestion lag began seven minutes after deduplication CPU crossed 90%.
A network dashboard showed elevated retransmits on one rack, but affected and unaffected workers were spread across several racks.

During the incident, workers still receiving the prior schema had allocation and GC-pause metrics near baseline, while adjacent workers processing the new schema remained elevated; traffic volume differed by less than 8% between the groups.
During an eight-minute deduplication-capacity increase, customer lag fell 19% while GC pauses and broker redeliveries were unchanged; incoming event rate also fell 12% during the same interval.
Extending broker leases to 30 s on a canary reduced redelivery by 82% while leaving decoder allocation and GC behavior unchanged.
Disabling deduplication in staging made duplicate downstream records visible during forced GC pauses.
Storage-write latency remained at baseline until after customer lag had already begun.
No heap profile was retained from the incident, so the specific object class responsible for the allocation increase is unknown.
One broker node reported 71% disk utilization during part of the incident, but redeliveries spanned partitions on broker nodes with normal disk utilization.

hypotheses.text: The new schema and decoder path initiated the worker memory-pressure change.
Broker redelivery was the initiating origin of the worker GC pauses.
Deduplication saturation mediated part of the path from redelivery to customer-visible lag.
Rack-level packet retransmission materially contributed to worker pauses during the incident.
A specific nested-attribute object class was the dominant source of the decoder allocation increase.
A 30-second broker lease would not delay recovery from unrelated worker-failure modes.

actions.text: Rollback or gate the new schema/decoder path while profiling the allocation increase.
Increase deduplication capacity during the incident.
Disable deduplication so the service cannot become saturated.
Extend broker leases enough to tolerate observed pauses while preserving redelivery safety.
Increase storage-write timeout because storage latency rose during the incident.
